title: Wolff reflects on impact of tow in Las Vegas Qualifying
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has explained how Mercedes learned about the effectiveness of the slipstream during Qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, with the Silver Arrows Team Principal believing George Russell had been ideally positioned to secure pole.

Mercedes enjoyed a strong session as Kimi Antonelli topped the timesheets ahead of Max Verstappen and Russell, but a five-place grid penalty for the Italian due to power unit changes means he will start sixth, promoting his team mate to the front row alongside the Dutchman.

The final stages of Qualifying saw drivers jostling for position to benefit from a tow along the circuit's lengthy straights, something Wolff explained had caught Mercedes by surprise.

"I've had 35 years in motorsport," Wolff told F1 TV. "I've never seen tows working when you're one and a half seconds behind each other like a train, because normally you should be penalised through the corners so much that the straights never compensate for it.

"But for whatever reason, here it seems to work. We found out later than some of the other teams, and I have no idea how these lap times came together."

Antonelli made the decision himself to drop to the back of the queue ahead of his final flying lap, with Mercedes initially concerned he wouldn't reach the line with enough time to start.

"We thought he wouldn't cross the line in time," Wolff explained. "But the truth is, even if he had, he would have been much too close to the car ahead of him, and so that lap for me was gone. And then, for whatever miracle reason, it was fast."

Speaking separately to Sky Sports F1, Wolff explained that he had expected Russell to be in contention for pole, although Mercedes still needed to investigate where the Briton had lost time.

"George, for me, had the perfect position. He was four seconds behind the car in front," Wolff said.

"We need to find out because I think there was something in Turns 7, 8 and 9, whether that was a mistake or something else happened. But it looked like the ideal position for a pole lap because he was quickest all the time."

Looking ahead to Russell starting alongside Verstappen, Wolff added: "Big cinema if they try to go through the first corners together. We shall be watching."

title: What are the tyre strategy options for the Las Vegas GP?
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli was quickest in Qualifying but a five-place grid drop means Max Verstappen inherited pole position in Las Vegas, but will he be able to convert that to victory on Saturday night?

Running in FP3 – our only dry practice session – suggested Red Bull and McLaren, while substantially quicker than Mercedes through the twisty middle sector, are losing almost a second to the Silver Arrows on the straights. The tow hid that in Qualifying, but in the race, it’s the sort of deficit that can shake-out an order pretty quickly.

That is, of course, if the race goes by the numbers – and frankly, the Las Vegas Strip Circuit just isn’t that sort of track. While offering ample overtaking opportunities, it is also capricious: low-grip, omnipresent walls, and perfectly able to supply a game-changing Safety Car, VSC or red flag. Taking the jackpot in Vegas requires a quick car and a solid plan. The quick car alone won’t be good enough.

title: What To Watch For in the Las Vegas Grand Prix
excerpt:
From an eye-catching front row to Ferrari trying to recover from Qualifying disappointment, and from drivers starting out of position due to grid penalties to a forecast for one of the coldest races in history, here are five things to keep an eye on ahead of a spectacular evening under the lights in Las Vegas…

1. Verstappen vs Russell

Robust racing had broken out between Max Verstappen and George Russell even before we reached a competitive session this weekend, as an incident in FP3 led to the pair having to visit the stewards.

Verstappen overtook Russell before Turn 14 but then the Mercedes driver came back at his rival on the brakes and there was light contact between the two cars.

title: Lindblad's Vegas Qualifying 'such a mess' despite P5 start
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad believes his Qualifying performance for the Las Vegas Grand Prix "was such a mess", despite the Racing Bulls driver set to start from fifth on the grid.

It was a good day for the Faenza outfit as Lindblad not only led the midfield battle but also outpaced one McLaren and both Ferraris, with the Formula 1 rookie gaining a further position as Kimi Antonelli serves a grid penalty.

Having not experienced the track until Thursday’s rain-affected running, Lindblad breezed through the three Qualifying sessions in P7, P6 and P6 while still learning by the lap.

“It's been a tricky day. Basically no laps yesterday, and on any street circuit, any limited running is always more of a challenge," he said.

"So I was having to build a lot throughout today, every lap trying to get more comfortable. Even during Qualifying, I was learning a lot with every lap. So happy with how I learned, how I built.

“[But] it was such a mess. The tyres weren't working, so I had a lot of understeer, I made a bit of a mistake in Turn 8. So it wasn't a perfect lap.

"Also, at the same time, there's a lot that's not gone my way the recent races that's been out of my control, and there's been times I have done very good laps, but due to things you haven't seen it. So I'll take the bit of luck."

Racing Bulls team mate Liam Lawson backed up his team mate with a solid P8 performance after rueing a loss of straight line speed on his final run.

Still it was a double Q3 appearance for the team who are looking to secure fifth in the Teams' standings, and that P8 grid slot will turn to P7 for the race as New Zealander will be promoted following Oscar Piastri's penalty.

"We had a very good car, very good corner speed today,” said the Kiwi.

“Just had no straight line speed, which here is just impossible. I don't really know why, I need to check whether it's something I did on battery usage, or I don't know.

“Honestly, there's not really much you can do. So I'll go and check. But yeah, it's a shame because I think the car was very, very good, and I feel like we did a good job today, and extracted everything out of it.”

title: What the teams said – Qualifying in Las Vegas
excerpt:
Mercedes

Russell topped FP3 and went into Qualifying as the favourite for pole. He was quick in Q1 and Q2 as well, while Antonelli only just scraped into the final segment in P10. But come Q3, Mercedes saw an about turn. Russell wanted a tow and was not happy with being sent out in free air, while Antonelli dropped back and let the whole field pass him.

Somehow, the Italian managed to sneak across the line with a second to go, and despite being tucked up in traffic, he put in a superb lap to grab the fastest time. But it was not pole for the World Champion due to his five-place grid penalty. Russell qualified third, but starts second after his team mate’s grid drop.

Kimi Antonelli, 1st, 1:33.893

"It was certainly a strange qualifying session! I struggled to get the tyres into the right window and didn’t have the feeling with the car that I wanted, so I honestly didn’t expect to end up fastest. On the final lap, several cars pushed past me so I had to back off and create some space to prepare the tyres. The communication with Bono was really good as we were incredibly tight on time, and I crossed the line with only around a second to spare. I then started the lap much closer to the car ahead than you would normally want, which made the corners difficult, but the tow was incredibly powerful on the straights and ultimately helped us get the fastest time. It was high-risk, but it worked out, so I’m happy with the result even if I wasn’t completely happy with my own performance.

"Of course, the grid penalty means we will start P6 tomorrow, but I felt more comfortable with the car on the long runs in FP3 than I did over a single lap. The tow is so strong here that I expect the field to stay close, so we will need to be smart with our overtaking and strategy. We have a good race car underneath us and the target is to fight our way forward and see if we can challenge for the win."

George Russell, 3rd, 1:34.224

"Overall, I’m pleased with how qualifying went. I’ve felt competitive on every lap this weekend and I feel like I’ve got the car beneath me. Of course, I would have loved to take pole, but I don’t think any of us anticipated just how powerful the slipstream would be. Everyone was looking for a tow in Q3 and nobody wanted to be at the front of the pack. Getting it right was very high-risk, though, as you had to leave it incredibly late to get the maximum benefit.

"Starting on the front row for the third race in a row is still a strong position to be in. With the tow being so powerful here, I think it will be difficult for anyone at the front to break away tomorrow. We saw something similar in Monza, so I expect a close and strategic race between several cars at the front. We’ve got good pace and we’re definitely in a position to fight for the win."

Toto Wolff, Head of Mercedes-Benz Motorsport

"That was an incredibly tight and unpredictable qualifying session. Kimi found a huge tow on his final lap and, although we thought he was far too close to the car ahead, somehow, he made it work to set the fastest time. George looked in a very strong position too; he had what seemed like the ideal gap and had been quickest throughout, but lost some time around Turns 7, 8 and 9. That was unfortunate but he will start on the front-row tomorrow so has every chance of fighting for victory this weekend.

"It should be an entertaining race and, even with Kimi starting P6 after his grid penalty, both cars can hopefully be fighting to be on the podium. With the cars at the front so closely matched, the opening corners could be thrilling to watch. That said, it will be a long race so hopefully we can get through the first lap cleanly and then put ourselves in the mix for the rest of the evening."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"We made the most of the learning opportunities in FP3, given it was our only chance to run on a dry track ahead of qualifying. After struggling in the wet yesterday, we were hoping to find the car in a better place today. The early laps of the long run looked sensible and, after a few small tweaks, the balance was reasonable. Our single lap potential also looked good, although some of our competitors didn’t get clean runs, so we expected qualifying to be very close.

"It ended up being quite a messy session for us. We underestimated the advantage of having a tow, but with nobody wanting to be at the front of the pack, positioning the cars with traffic ahead was far from straightforward. George ended up with a reasonable gap for his final effort, while Kimi was at risk of missing the flag and had to start his lap just 1.4 seconds behind Lindblad. We thought that proximity had cost him any chance of improving, so we were both pleased and a little surprised when he managed to go fastest.

"Kimi’s Power Unit penalty drops him back to P6, but with George starting P2, we should be well placed to fight at the front tomorrow. Overtaking looks possible with the long straights and relatively low levels of tyre overheating, so it should make for an interesting race."

title: Alpine left disappointed despite Gasly’s ‘perfect’ Q2 lap
excerpt:
A Las Vegas GP Qualifying session that briefly promised much more ended in disappointment for Alpine as Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto finished at the bottom of Q3 in P9 and P10.

Having been second fastest on intermediates in Thursday’s FP2 session, Gasly again popped up in P2 after a superb lap in Q2.

Given that he took pole at Monza on a track also dominated by long straights, it looked like he might once again at least mix it with the cars from the established frontrunning teams.

However, in what was a messy Q3 session that saw several drivers tripping over each other ahead of the final runs, he wasn’t able to repeat that form, and he had to settle for P9.

“I think Q2 was pretty much the perfect track position, out lap, prep lap, and the way everything sort of worked out,” said the Frenchman. “Tried to do the same in Q3, and unfortunately, it didn't quite work out the same way.

“I think in that first run, there were definitely a few things we could have managed better as a team. But yeah, I think we'll review it all to get stronger and work well. In that second run, it was just a bit, I would say, unlucky, and all these cars bunched up. I had to slow down, open the gap, cold tyres into Turn 1.

“I lost two or three tenths into the first sector, and that was... I feel like at least a position was on the table. I lost by a hundredth to Lawson. So that was clearly at least one position more to get.”

Gasly was sure that he could have finished further up the order, even if a Monza repeat was never on the cards.

“It did feel like everything kind of worked out perfectly [in Q2],” he said. “And I was hoping we at least can get the same, which I think would have put us with Hadjar, like P6 or something like that, in front of Lindblad.

“But honestly, the tow was insane. If you look at the last sector of Antonelli, you just understand how powerful. I've never, ever felt that in a car. So yeah, there was a lot down to that. Unfortunately, it just didn't quite work as we wanted.”

Colapinto, meanwhile, was an encouraging P7 in Q2 but, like Gasly, he also had a difficult final session and thus had to settle for P10.

“I think we are all very disappointed,” he admitted. “The last run was a mess. The previous one, I just took a bit of a feel. I was fully alone on track. So in the straights, I was very slow. But I think the pace was generally there. We had a few places where we could do better and we could improve.

“But the session was just very up and down. Like, some laps you had grip, some laps not. And then the last lap, with all the mess in the prep lap, having a bit of a, of a race together, was not good. So the tyres were not in a good place.

“The lap was nowhere in terms of sector one: no grip, sliding everywhere, tyres very far out the window. And that here matters a lot when you don't do things correctly because of traffic or positioning. You pay it really hard later on in the lap.”

Like Gasly, he stressed the value of the tow: “You probably lose around eight/nine tenths in the straights only with no tows. It's big, and that means in the race it's going to be fun because it's going to create some moves.

“But in quali, it's tricky because you want to be behind someone, but you want also a good prep lap. And if people in front are not doing what you want, then it becomes a real mess.

“It was a pity because I think no run was maximised, so then you always have this feeling that could have been a lot better. But it is what it is – we have to focus on tomorrow.”

title: Russell stunned by 'insane’ tow power in Las Vegas
excerpt:
George Russell has admitted that he was surprised by the “insane” tow power in Qualifying at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, with the Mercedes racer set to start from the front row for Saturday’s race despite not benefitting from a slipstream as others did.

After topping the timesheets earlier on in the weekend’s third and final practice hour, Russell again looked to have good pace in Qualifying.

However, the Briton emerged on track in front of team mate Kimi Antonelli – who was set to serve a five-place grid penalty – during the first runs of Q3, meaning that he could not get a tow from the other Silver Arrows machine.

While he asked over the radio if he could go behind Antonelli, given the World Champion’s impending penalty, the squad ultimately did not use a tow – with Antonelli dropping back during the final runs and only just making the flag to start his lap, one that ultimately put him in P1 before his grid drop demoted him to P6.

Russell, meanwhile, went third fastest behind Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, meaning that he will start from P2 behind the Dutchman in Saturday’s race.

“It was a very strong session on the whole, but of course it came down to that slipstream and I don't think any of us anticipated how powerful it would be,” Russell reflected after Qualifying.

“It was insane. I still can't wrap my head around it. Kimi said he gained over one second to himself from the lap before, just in the straights.

"But it's high risk – if he started his lap just a few seconds later, he would have had no lap at all, so in the end I'm pleased with the session as a whole.”

Looking ahead to race day, the 28-year-old believes that a number of drivers could be in the fight for victory.

“I think it's going to be very close out there tomorrow,” Russell explained. “As I said, with the slipstream being so powerful, I think it's going to very challenging for the lead car, whoever it may be, to get away, so I think any drivers in the top five or six will be in contention.”

title: Antonelli's 'big risk' pays off in Vegas Qualifying
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli admits that he "took a big risk" after finishing fastest in Qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, with the Mercedes driver also suggesting "I wasn't driving well".

The World Champion finished top of the times during Qualifying on Friday, beating Red Bull's Max Verstappen by just over two tenths.

But the Italian will start sixth for Saturday's Grand Prix after serving a five-place grid penalty for a turbo change ahead of the weekend.

Antonelli's fastest time came at the very end of the session, having only just made it onto his final flying lap as he and other drivers battled for position, with the tow proving especially effective along the Strip.

It meant Antonelli began his lap close to the car ahead, with the 20-year-old also struggling for grip throughout, making his efforts to finish P1 even more of a surprise.

When asked how satisfied he was with Qualifying, Antonelli responded: "Not really to be fair because I had no feeling with the car today in single lap."

"I couldn't get the tyres in the right window and was just really... I had zero confidence. I wasn't driving well, [I made] lots of mistakes.

"And that last lap I took a big risk, decided to back off and it's never ideal when you start the lap so close to the car in front because with the dirty air you slide a lot around. But overall it worked out and I'm happy with it."

The last time Antonelli served a grid penalty for a power unit change was in Italy, with the Mercedes driver storming through the field from P19 on the grid to take victory at home.

With Las Vegas' street circuit also offering the chance for overtakes, and with Antonelli only starting from P6, he remains hopeful of a strong result come the end of the Grand Prix.

"Definitely," said Antonelli when asked about fighting for a top result.

"I've been feeling more comfortable in long run, especially in FP3 so hopefully tomorrow we can get a good start and fight back and hopefully we can get a great result."

title: Norris expects tough Vegas GP amid McLaren speed struggles
excerpt:
Lando Norris has admitted he expects a "tough day" in the Las Vegas Grand Prix, despite securing a second-row start, with the McLaren driver concerned that a lack of straight-line speed could hamper his chances in the race.

The Briton was fourth fastest during a closely fought Qualifying session on the streets of Las Vegas, finishing just 0.020s behind Mercedes' George Russell and less than a tenth adrift of Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

With newly-crowned World Champion Kimi Antonelli set to take a five-place grid penalty after topping the timesheets, Norris will be promoted to third on the grid, starting alongside Isack Hadjar, behind polesitter Verstappen and Russell.

Despite McLaren struggling to match their rivals on the straights, Norris was satisfied with his performance, having made the most of the slipstream around the high-speed circuit.

"It felt pretty good, honestly," he said. "I'm very happy with my lap. I really couldn't get much more out of it.

"We just struggle a lot here on the straights, like an insane amount. So there's not much more we can do, but I think we made the most of it, with the slipstreams. But we just have a deficit at the moment."

With Thursday's wet practice sessions limiting representative running, Norris was less certain about McLaren's prospects for the Grand Prix, particularly when it comes to overtaking.

"We didn't learn much, so we have to see how tomorrow goes," he explained. "Honestly, I don't know.

"The pace in the car is not bad. The car is performing well, but our straight-line speed is just so far off that we're not going to even be able to overtake someone. So I think it's going to be a tough day."

Meanwhile, team mate Oscar Piastri qualified seventh after an improved showing compared to practice, although a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding his allocation of internal combustion engines will see the Australian start from P17.

"I just drove better, to be honest," the Australian driver said of his improvement from practice to Qualifying. "I didn't do a great job in practice this morning. I think Qualifying was better. Q3 was still messy, for sure, but ultimately, I'm reasonably happy.

"Trying to get the right slipstream is so important, and it seems so sensitive. I was just a little bit further back on my second lap, and I lost so much time down the straights."

With plenty of ground to make up, Piastri has set his sights on recovering into the points, although he acknowledged that the closely matched field could make progress difficult.

"I think getting back into the points is definitely the biggest aim, clearly," he added. "I think qualifying showed that with slipstreams and stuff, a lot of people are at a very similar pace. So I'm not sure how easy it's going to be tomorrow, but we'll try."

title: Ferrari drivers critical of 'very poor Qualifying' in Vegas
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc admits that he and Ferrari team mate Lewis Hamilton suffered "a very poor Qualifying" for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, as both drivers were eliminated from Q2.

Leclerc finished just over one-tenth adrift of making the final part of Qualifying on Friday evening, with Hamilton half a second away from making the cut as the pair finished P11 and P12 respectively.

"Just a very poor Qualifying. We are losing one second in the straights, which makes it difficult enough already," said Leclerc, who will start P10 after a grid penalty for Oscar Piastri ahead.

"Then I did a mistake when I had to put the lap in in Q2, following I think multiple mistakes we've done as a team, and we need to look at that because that builds a lot of frustration that then doesn't help.

"But at the end of the day, it's on me on the mistake and I'll look at that, but not much more to add.

"Unfortunately I'm very hopeless for tomorrow because we are losing one second down the straight, so there's nothing we can do."

Ferrari's lack of straight line speed was not helped as neither driver was able to find a tow at the crucial moment, an aspect which proved imperative for the rest of the field during the session.

Track temperatures were also incredibly low at only 15C, with Hamilton admitting he struggled for grip having gone into the run-off area at Turn 1 at one stage.

"It was a nightmare. It's like… just low grip. It felt like the tyres weren't working," said the seven-time World Champion, who will start P11.

"We had some damage on the floor that appeared out of nowhere, which was losing three or four tenths, and then we had the deployment issue on the last lap, which lost us six tenths, so with that we were just nowhere. And I had no one ahead of me, so that wasn't also great, so just a combination of everything not being great.

"It makes it a little bit tougher for us to progress [in the race] and it's hard to do a lot from where we are. We knew that we would struggle a little bit here, but maybe a little more than we anticipated."

title: McLaren explain how a plastic bag derailed surprising Lando Norris attack
excerpt:
McLaren boss Andrea Stella has detailed how a plastic bag wrecked Lando Norris's surprising bid for pole position at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Norris qualified fourth on the road for round 21 of the season, but will be promoted to third after qualifying winner Kimi Antonelli lost his pole position due to the five-place grid drop he was already carrying for a new ICE.

Max Verstappen and George Russell are therefore promoted to the front-row, with Norris 0.093s behind Verstappen and 0.020s slower than Russell on a track not expected to suit McLaren's MCL40 machine.

The car is known to be draggy, with McLaren opting for shorter gear ratios than other front-running teams, meaning the car lacks top-end straight-line speed.

However, with the aid of the slipstream from other cars, Norris was able to produce a lap-time which has put him at the sharp end of the grid, and in the prime position to take over the lead should anything befall Verstappen and Russell on the opening lap after their feud restarted in FP3.

In his media briefing at the end of the day, team principal Stella revealed how a plastic bag had got stuck in Norris's floor in the session, potentially costing a tenth of a second in performance - about the margin Norris was behind Verstappen, who inherited pole.

During the second free practice session on Thursday, a brief red flag was flown after a plastic wrap made its way onto the track, which was then run over by Aston Martin's Lance Stroll, with other small debris, such as crisp packets, also blowing on the racing surface - which is opened to the public after the cessation of track activities.

"If anything, we could have been even more competitive in qualifying, especially on Lando's side," Stella began to media, including RacingNews365.

"He was quite unlucky because a plastic bag got stuck in the floor and we lost quite a lot of downforce.

"So considering that one-tenth of a second would make a big difference, and there certainly was a tenth of a second in a plastic bag, which is a bit of a shame.

"But we need to look at how we keep the car raceable in the race.

"If we look at Monza, we saw that with the towing effect you can actually stay tangled and linked to the other cars.

"So we are definitely looking forward [to the race] and are encouraged by the fact that qualifying has been competitive."

[Article continues below]

McLaren' straight-line speed problems

Turning to the straight-line speed woes the team has had in 2026, Stella praised the efforts to ensure Norris and Oscar Piastri were placed in the queue of cars accordingly to enable them to have the best access to the powerful tow.

"We definitely had some concerns in terms of how suitable the demands of this circuit would be for the car at high speed," he added.

"It is not only the top speed, but it is also the top speed that combines with the tow, so you go into operating regimes of the engine that, with our ratios, are not ideal.

"We know that the drag, from an aerodynamic point of view, is not a point of trend, but we discuss in the debrief that we need to look holistically at all the conditions that influence the top speed.

"But certainly, we have seen here traits that are similar to Monza and Baku, and in all conditions, we were not particularly competitive.

"I think what we have done better here is to mitigate this by having really good positioning in qualifying. The car was pretty much where we wanted it to be in qualifying, and this definitely helped because I have to say that it seems like, with these regulations, the drag reduction when you follow one car or even multiple cars is more than in the past, and therefore there's an even higher incentive to be positioned in the right place."

title: Exclusive: Oliver Bearman exploring shock move to F1 rival as Haas contract delay rumbles on
excerpt:
Oliver Bearman could be on the brink of a remarkable end to the F1 season, which would see him leave Haas, sever ties with Ferrari, and potentially join a Formula 1 rival, RacingNews365 understands.

Bearman is the last remaining driver on the F1 grid yet to be confirmed for next season. The Briton and Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu have expressed confidence over the past few weeks that the matter would be resolved and the partnership would continue.

However, according to sources, Bearman remains in limbo as he and his management have long expected the 21-year-old to race for Ferrari next year following two highly successful seasons at Haas where he has enjoyed exemplary treatment over that time, notably with unswerving support from team principal Komatsu.

The path to hoped-for promotion, however, is naturally blocked by Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton. The seven-time F1 champion revealed in his media session on Wednesday ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix that he is only “halfway” through his contract and that he has every intention of seeing it through.

Bearman's situation is further complicated by the fact he now has another Ferrari Academy driver product, Rafael Camara, as his team-mate after the Brazilian impressed in a recent shootout and was chosen to replace the axed Esteban Ocon.

Bearman’s management, however, is apparently unwilling to take the risk of Camara dealing a blow to their driver, just as Bearman did to Ocon, against all prior expectations, and they are now looking for a way out of his current ties.

That is the real reason a new contract has not been signed until now.

In Las Vegas, in an interview with F1TV, Bearman, who had always previously emphasised that a new deal was imminent, changed tone and gave the impression the situation was out of his hands, and that any new contract could be finalised at any moment.

According to our sources, this new narrative serves multiple purposes: on one hand, it attempts to shift the blame onto other parties in the eyes of the public, and on the other, it paves the way for the move they are hoping for - a split.

[Article continues below]

Where does Bearman go?

In Bearman’s situation, the only acceptable move is to secure a race seat immediately for 2027 somewhere outside Ferrari’s sphere of influence.

The driver’s representatives have explored numerous options since the summer: there have been whispers in the paddock of talks held with Mercedes and McLaren, as well as Aston Martin, at a time when there was a possibility Fernando Alonso could retire at the end of the season. RacingNews365 understands that discussions also took place with Williams.

Now, only one strictly theoretical option remains: Alpine.

The Enstone-based outfit previously indicated that Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto would again form their driver lineup in 2027, but a lot has happened since the Argentine driver’s contract was announced on August 27th.

In the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, a reckless overtaking manoeuvre from Colapinto on Gasly resulted in the retirement of both cars. Although Colapinto regretted the incident, word around the team is that the atmosphere changed after that moment of madness.

Internal morale has also not been helped by the toxic environment created by Colapinto's fanbase on social media, forcing the team into continual explanations.

Sources have indicated that the trust previously placed in Colapinto by Flavio Briatore, Alpine’s executive advisor and de facto leader, has wavered following the incident with Gasly, allied to his inconsistent performances.

Briatore is renowned as a pragmatic manager who has, on countless occasions throughout his career, proven that no driver's seat is bulletproof and that he does not hesitate to act when a situation demands.

RacingNews365 understands that Bearman’s management is trying to capitalise on this. Multiple meetings have taken place between Bearman’s representatives and Briatore - in the paddock and in Monaco where Bearman and the team leader are living.

As to whether a deal will happen depends on whether complex contractual issues will be resolved, whilst any potential agreement also requires a substantial financial package from the British driver.

Colapinto’s main sponsor, Mercado Libre, reportedly pays Alpine at least $20 million. If the Bearman camp has managed to put together a similar package, Briatore could easily decide to pull the trigger.

With expectations set to rise following the arrival of new title sponsor Gucci next year, industry experts consulted by RacingNews365 believe a Gasly–Bearman pairing would offer completely different optics than the current one.

As for Colapinto, he could remain at Alpine as third driver, a role vacant after Paul Aron recently departed.

It cannot be ruled out that he would move heaven and earth to return to Williams. There has been talk in the paddock of late about an increase in meetings between the driver and team principal James Vowles, who recently answered "yes" in an interview when asked if he could imagine Colapinto returning to the Grove-based team in the future.

The matter is likely to drag on for a while longer, and a final decision may not materialise until the winter break.

title: Kimi Antonelli scolded for 'nasty' George Russell ploy: 'He will be really upset'
excerpt:
Jacques Villeneuve has accused Kimi Antonelli of deliberately denying George Russell a tow during Q3 of qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, despite the Italian starting being unable to get pole position due to a grid penalty.

Antonelli set the fastest lap of the session, a 1:33.893, but will start the race from sixth after a five-place grid penalty for fitting a sixth internal combustion engine of the season.

Max Verstappen therefore inherits pole position, with his Mercedes team-mate promoted to second after lapping in 1:34.224.

Russell found himself at the head of a long train of cars on his final run, including both Racing Bulls, the two Alpines and Antonelli, who trailed at the back, benefiting fully from the draft down the Strip.

The F1 drivers' champion later admitted over team radio that his lap was "all tow", with telemetry showing a 16 km/h straight-line speed advantage over the Briton.

Asked about the sequence on Sky Sports F1, Toto Wolff defended Mercedes' approach, insisting Russell had not been short-changed.

"Actually, George, for me, had the perfect position. He was four seconds behind the car in front," the Mercedes team principal said.

"We need to find out because I think there was some kind of… turn seven-eight-nine, whether that was a mistake or something else happened, we need to… I don’t know, to be honest, but it looked like the ideal position for a pole lap, because he was quickest all the time."

[Article continues below]

Villeneuve takes aim at Antonelli

Villeneuve, speaking on the same broadcast, rejected that explanation outright, highlighting the need to help Russell in his bid for second in the drivers' standings, and taking aim at Antonelli's tactics.

Antonelli leads on 390 points, having already sealed the title, with Verstappen second on 279 and Russell third on 262, 17 points behind the Red Bull driver with three rounds remaining.

"The team didn’t do anything to help Russell," Villeneuve said. "When Toto says Russell was four seconds behind and he was in a good position, that was from his [Russell's] doing. The team did not help him.

"He kind of skirted the answer there because Kimi went out of his way to make sure he wasn’t ahead of Russell, to make sure he wouldn’t help his team-mate, and that was obvious.

"He played his own card; he played his own game even though he knew that he couldn’t get pole in the end.

"That was a little bit nasty, and George will be really, really upset. Mostly when Antonelli has got the world championship, the team has got the championship; they had every interest in helping George."

title: Las Vegas starting grid heavily adjusted after FIVE driver penalties
excerpt:
Max Verstappen and George Russell will share the front-row for the Las Vegas Grand Prix after Kimi Antonelli was demoted from pole position.

Antonelli was carrying a five-place grid penalty for a new ICE, but still won qualifying over Verstappen and Russell, who were both called to the stewards for an incident in FP3.

Both escaped with a warning, but given their history, it makes for a tantalising opening lap during Saturday evening's local time grand prix.

Lando Norris is third from Isack Hadjar, with Arvid Lindblad a career-best fifth.

Elsewhere, Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton are only 10th and 11th for Ferrari after a double Q2 elimination, whilst Oscar Piastri, Carlos Sainz, Lance Stroll, and Oliver Bearman have all taken engine-related penalties and thus drop down the order.

title: Oliver Bearman makes Haas demand after 'scary' experience: 'We’ve got a big issue'
excerpt:
Haas saw both of their drivers suffer dramatic spins at Turn 1 on Friday at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Oliver Bearman has stated there is a "big issue" with his Haas car after suffering a "scary" spin on Friday in Las Vegas.

At the end of final practice, Bearman found himself turned around at Turn 1 after suddenly losing the car under braking.

A couple of hours later in qualifying, his team-mate Rafael Câmara had a similar issue after losing the car without warning at the first corner.

Bearman has called on Haas to get to the root of the issue to avoid a repeat of the incident during Saturday night's grand prix.

"We've got a big issue with the car," Bearman told media, including RacingNews365. "It was the strangest spin ever. Rafa had the same thing in quali.

"We need to work on our brake maps or something, because it's pretty scary going into Turn 1 and you're not sure if you're going to spin or not.

"I just braked and I felt the car wasn't quite slowing down. Next thing I know, I'm looking back at the last corner, which is a bit scary."

Bearman spin was 'like nothing I've ever experienced before'

Bearman will start Sunday's race from the back of the grid due to an engine-related grid penalty.

His low grid position presents him with an uphill battle to add to his points tally this year, a prospect further hindered by Bearman's lack of confidence in the car.

"When I spun it, I was on new tyres, and Rafa was the same," he said.

"It's to do with our qualifying engine map and how the rear brakes interact with the MGU-K, and how that interaction is.

"We've missed the trick there. It's a pretty unique track, this one, because of the short run down to Turn 1.

"It means that we rely a lot on the rear brakes in Turn 1, which we've never had to do before, and we clearly have an issue with our maps, because that spin I had was like nothing I've ever experienced in a car before in my life."

title: Lando Norris demands McLaren fix after 'horrendous' handicap exposed
excerpt:
Lando Norris has demanded McLaren find a fix for its ongoing issues with straight-line speed after an "horrendous" experience in Las Vegas qualifying.

Norris will start third on the grid in Sin City, having qualified fourth on the road but will be promoted one spot due to Kimi Antonelli's five-place demotion from pole to sixth for a new ICE.

Norris was 0.351s slower than Antonelli, with the Mercedes receiving a monster tow from Arvid Lindblad's Racing Bulls to earn around 16kph more speed than the sister W17 of George Russell.

However, Norris and McLaren's MCL40 machine has struggled all season with pure straight-line speed, with the car known to be draggy.

This is for a number of factors, including a shorter wheelbase than the other top teams and also shorter gear ratios which limit the top-end grunt available for Norris and Oscar Piastri.

Reflecting on his session, Norris detailed the challenge he was having to overcome with the deficit in a straight line, something he branded "horrendous" and "awful" and which made it "impossible to fight" for higher positions.

However, his team principal Andrea Stella then revealed that a plastic bag got trapped in the floor during the session, costing around a tenth of a second in lap-time - with Norris 0.093s behind Max Verstappen, who inherited pole.

"We're just shocking on the straights, like horrendous in the straights," Norris told media, including RacingNews365.

"So my lap was very good; it was easily my best lap, but to Kimi, we're eight-tenths off in the last sector.

"He had a perfect tow and did a very good job, but compared to most other people, we're just too far off.

"I have to start my lap 1.5s behind the car ahead, which means in every corner I'm losing at least half a tenth to a tenth because of the downforce I am losing. There is obviously a bigger gain in having a good slipstream, but we've had to make up for a pretty terrible loss of straight-line speed.

"Therefore, we have to harm our cornering speed, so we just haven't got the right balance all in all in terms of downforce vs drag.

"So it has made our life impossible to fight, and obviously it's been an issue all year."

When then asked if the lack of speed was down to how long the Vegas Strip straight is, Norris rejected the idea.

"You can't blame the straights; it is just that our car is not good," he said.

"We have to improve that a lot, and you cannot fight at Monza, here, or Baku. We're bad because we're just awful on the straights, and we have to improve it for next year."

[Article continues below]

Norris on slipstream effect

Turning to the importance of the slipstream, Norris spoke of the balancing act required to ace the effect.

"Very [difficult], because it is not as simple as it seems," he said.

"You don't just gain from it because you then have a bigger gap to the car ahead after you pass, so it is better to be in the pack in a slipstream from a lot of people.

"But even with that, we still lose eight-tenths in the final sector, so it is something you can do, but here, it doesn't necessarily work because you have a lot of straights.

"So it is better just to be in the flow of three or four cars."

title: Toto Wolff 'has no clue' how Kimi Antonelli was able to pull off impossible F1 lap
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has explained that he and Mercedes "have absolutely no clue" how Kimi Antonelli was able to pull off the fastest lap in Las Vegas Grand Prix qualifying.

The Italian was fastest in qualifying in Sin City, setting a 1:33.893, but he will not start on pole position for the eighth time owing to a five-place grid penalty for a new ICE component.

He will drop to sixth, with Max Verstappen thus being credited with pole position, but Antonelli's lap was in doubt as he made it to the line to start his final flying lap with just one second remaining on the clock after being caught in a fuffle akin to Q3 at the 2019 Italian GP as the field tried to ensure they were not at the head of the train - and thus give the tow to rivals.

Antonelli was ultimately at the back of the pack, but in starting his lap, was tucked right up behind the Racing Bulls machine of Arvid Lindblad - ideal for the tow in straight lines, but not in the corners as Lindblad's car threw dirty air out the back.

However, Antonelli was still able to roar to the fastest time, 0.258s faster than Verstappen - with the tow making up 16kph for the Italian.

"We have absolutely no clue," Wolff told Sky Sports F1 after Antonelli's final lap about how it was possible to achieve it.

"We thought Kimi was going to miss the lap or he was going to be way too close to Lindblad.

"He crossed the line 1.4s behind, and that was basically it.

"I don't understand how, being that close [to another car], you can even do this time.

"If you are 1.4s behind the car in front, you would think this is too close, especially [to a car] that went eight-tenths slower.

"But for whatever reason, it works."

[Article continues below]

Russell's session

Turning to Russell, who had asked for the tow to be given to him, given Antonelli's penalty, Wolff felt the Briton was in the prime place for a good lap - as he took third on the road, and will start second once Antonelli's penalty is applied.

"Actually, George, for me, had a perfect position; he was four seconds behind the car in front, and we need to find out because I think there was something around Turns 7, 8, 9, a mistake or something happened," he said.

"It looked like the ideal position for a pole lap because he was the quickest all the time."

Turning to the Verstappen-Russell front row, after their latest spat in FP3 that prompted a stewards' inquiry, Wolff wryly predicted, "cinema, and if they try to go through the first corners together, we shall be watching."

title: Liam Lawson expresses 'buried' fear after stressful Las Vegas experience
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has explained how not having a tow in qualifying at the Las Vegas Grand Prix would leave a driver "buried" following chaotic scenes in the dying moments of Q3.

Lawson was ultimately eighth-quickest in the grid-setting session in Nevada, but will line up for the 50-lap race in seventh after Oscar Piastri's 10-place penalty for a power unit change.

The New Zealander also raised question marks over his lack of straight-line speed down The Strip, with Racing Bulls team-mate Arvid Lindblad, who starts fifth, four tenths of a second faster overall.

"We had a very good car, very good corner speed today. Just no straight-line speed, which here is just impossible," Lawson told media, including RacingNews365.

"I don't really know why. I need to check whether it's something I did on battery usage or I don't know, honestly.

"There's not really much you can do. So I'll go and check, but it's a shame because I think the car was very, very good, and I feel like we did a good job today. Extracted everything out of it."

In the closing stages of Q3, Lawson and Lindblad were two of six cars all seen squabbling for track position, alongside the two Mercedes and both Alpines.

Asked whether the traffic complicated matters, the 24-year-old agreed, highlighting the added jeopardy of getting a final timed effort in before the chequered flag.

"It was definitely making things difficult. Everyone's trying to get their lap, obviously. So yeah, trying to get all the right tow," he added.

"We were a little bit stressed about timings as well, but in the end, we were safe, so it was alright."

[Article continues below]

The fear of being 'buried'

It was put to Lawson that qualifying in Sin City had all the crucial variables of an F1 grid-setting session, just amplified due to the circuit configuration and difficulties with tyre temperature in the cold conditions.

"It definitely is," he replied. "You could do the world's best lap, but if you have no tow, I feel like you're just buried.

"There was a point in Q2 where I went out for my second run on a new set of tyres, and I went like six tenths slower, and I was up on my lap before Turn 12, just lost everything down the straight.

"So it's basically trying to get the right tow, and then for us, we have some question marks on why my last lap in Q3 was just not very strong down The Strip. So yeah, [we will] go and figure it out."

title: Charles Leclerc 'frustration building' as mistakes wreck 'painful' Las Vegas qualifying
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc cut a disheartened figure after a torrid qualifying session for Ferrari at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, where he and Lewis Hamilton were eliminated in Q2.

Whilst his team-mate lacked the required pace, errors proved more costly for Leclerc, who did not get a clean first effort and narrowly missed the opportunity to set a final timed lap, instead taking the chequered flag.

Having been P11 and P12 quickest, respectively, the Scuderia drivers will be handed a slight reprieve by way of Oscar Piastri's 10-place grid penalty, so are expected to line up for the 50-lap race in P10 and P11.

Reflecting on the grid-setting session, Leclerc outlined his dissatisfaction, highlighting how messy his evening in Sin City was.

"I'm very disappointed as a whole," the Monegasque driver told media, including RacingNews365. "Of course, there's the mistake in Q2 that we paid the price for, but I think that is following a lot of frustration building up with a lot of mistakes in the way we managed everything — traffic and other things.

"And that doesn't help particularly on a track like this where it's all about tyres; you've got to put tyres in the right window.

"I was more looking in my mirrors and trying to understand the traffic myself, and that makes it very difficult to do anything. So just very disappointed.

"We were expecting [it], [but] we lost one second down the straight, which is crazy. It's expected, and that makes it very, very difficult after that to recover anything.

"At the end [of qualifying], no Ferrari power unit. On a track like this, it is the most power-sensitive track of the season, so we expected to have a hard time, but I was expecting to go through Q3, though."

[Article continues below]

Too early to apportion blame

Leclerc explained he was not yet sure of the reason for the lack of communication and information from the Ferrari pit wall, and stressed that it is too early to assign blame, given the team was experiencing issues outside of its control during FP3.

"I don't know what the reason was for that today. I know this morning we had a lot of problems with GPS," the nine-time grand prix winner said.

"If that was a problem today, then it's understandable. But otherwise, we just need to make sure that in those critical moments we get everything right."

When put to him at this stage, Ferrari should not be making so many errors and should be more cohesive, Leclerc replied: "Again, before commenting further, I think we need to look at what the issue is today.

"If it's a GPS issue, which doesn't necessarily come from us, then it's something that we cannot do much about, and today was painful.

"But if it comes from us, I do agree we need to look at it and obviously improve, because particularly in the critical moments like this, we need to be there, and we weren't."

title: George Russell reignites fiery Max Verstappen feud: 'Someone has to stand up to that guy'
excerpt:
George Russell has spoken out about the incident he had with Max Verstappen at the end of final practice in Las Vegas.

In the closing stages of the session, Verstappen overtook Russell as they approached Turn 14.

However, as Russell looked to shift back in front of Verstappen, the four-time champion appeared to move across in front of Russell, causing the Mercedes driver to take avoiding action.

The two then went side-by-side into the braking zone, resulting in contact and an investigation from the stewards.

No penalty was handed out, however Verstappen was given a warning for his role in the skirmish, a punishment Russell believes was apt.

"I think a warning was fine," Russell told Sky F1.

"But there's nothing in the rules to say you can't overtake someone who is starting a lap.

"When you do this, you are screwing this person over. He does this week in, week out with many drivers, and everybody accepts it.

"I'm not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they're bigger and better than everyone else.

“Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

[Article continues below]

Russell backs permanent stewards decision

Verstappen has been in the wars during practice sessions in recent times, clashing with Liam Lawson last month at hte Mexico City Grand Prix.

The Dutchman is no stranger to his squabbles with Russell, who had a dramatic war of words with Verstappen through the media at the end of 2024.

The latest incident between the pair comes at a time when the FIA is seeking to implement a pool of permanent stewards from next year to bring about more consistency.

It's a decision that has been backed by Russell.

"On the stewards topic, I think permanent stewards are absolutely the right decision, so that's good,” he said.

title: Lewis Hamilton reveals cause behind shock Las Vegas qualifying early exit
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has revealed that a variety of issues with his Ferrari car resulted in an early exit from qualifying at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Hamilton appeared to struggle throughout the weekend in Las Vegas, particularly on Friday night in final practice and qualifying, when he suffered a number of lock-up moments that forced him wide.

However, a shocking double exit in Q2 did not appear to be a realistic possibility throughout the weekend, with Charles Leclerc also dropping out after making a mistake on his last push lap.

Hamilton detailed that his primary issue related to his floor, telling media including RacingNews365: “We lost a piece of the floor on the first or second lap of Q1, and the car balance shifted.

“We lost three or four tenths of downforce. After that, we were struggling, more so with sliding.”

Hamilton's day got even more challenging when he also suffered a deployment issue on his final lap, which he stated put the final nail in the coffin.

“My last lap was really good at the end, but I did the best I could with what I had,” he said.

“But then we lost something like six-tenths or something. With that, we would have been in Q3.

“But otherwise I was happy with my lap.”

[Article continues below]

Hamilton surprised by straight-line deficit

Ferrari has consistently struggled to keep up with its rivals on the straights this year, and knew that it would be limited in Las Vegas.

However, Hamilton admitted the gap was larger than he expected.

“We knew long straights were going to be challenging,” he said.

“The gap seems to be a little bit more than I anticipated in a straight line. It's not insignificant, it's a big chunk on the straights.

“Grip-wise, just didn't feel like we had a tonne of grip, and were struggling to get the tyres working. We were just kind of nowhere.”

title: Max Verstappen nursing lingering F1 car issue in Las Vegas pole surprise
excerpt:
Max Verstappen said he was struggling with elements of the car during Las Vegas qualifying that had also been present last time out in Brazil.

Early on in the day, Verstappen was heard complaining about his steering rack and the challenges he was facing behind the wheel.

Verstappen ended the qualifying session in second place but will be promoted to P1 on Saturday night's grid due to a grid penalty for Kimi Antonelli, who set the fastest time in Q3.

It puts the Dutchman in a strong position for Saturday night's grand prix as he goes in search of his third win in Las Vegas.

"[I was] just struggling with some things that were also in the car in Brazil, just trying to get my head around it to try and make the best out of it this weekend again," Verstappen explained.

"We had a solid qualifying. We executed well. My first lap in Q3 was pretty much as good as it can be, with the tow effect as well around the lap.

"To be on the front row is very good for us."

In the final moments of Q3, the cars fought for track position as they all looked to benefit from the slipstream.

Verstappen said it made the session very difficult to manage.

"Track temp, being in the right position, it's incredibly hard when you have so many straights around here.

"But I think we executed well, so we can be very happy with that."

title: Kimi Antonelli reveals 'screwed' fear in chaotic end to Las Vegas qualifying
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli was worried he was "screwed" during a messy conclusion to qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Antonelli crossed the line with only a second to spare after he and George Russell were seen jostling for track position with the Alpines and two Racing Bulls drivers before their final timed efforts.

His Mercedes nonetheless went fastest in the grid-setting session under the lights in Sin City, making use of a strong tow to gain 16kph over his team-mate down the back straight.

However, the young Italian has a five-place penalty to take after an engine change in the back of his W17.

He will therefore start sixth on the grid, behind Max Verstappen on pole, Russell, Lando Norris, Isack Hadjar and Arvid Lindblad.

"It felt like going back to 60 mini cars where you do the qualifying all together, all super close," the F1 drivers' champion said in Nevada.

"It was very weird qualifying for me. First of all, I couldn't get the tyres working, just zero feeling with the car, and also the brake pedal was very long, so I was struggling with the braking.

"But all in all, it was so unexpected, and on that last lap, I thought I was screwed because I started one second from the car in front, but the tow is so big here that I was able to just gain with that and put it on pole."

The 20-year-old was pleased with the performance of the Mercedes package during his long runs in the FP3, the only representative practice session, and did not count out fighting for victory despite the grid penalty.

"I feel like the race pace was strong in free practice," Antonelli added. "It felt good, and the tyres seemed in a good place, so I think we have a good chance tomorrow to fight for, hopefully, the win.

"But now we'll try to work, understand where we can do better, and come back stronger tomorrow."

title: Max Verstappen inherits Las Vegas pole as Ferrari suffer double elimination embarrassment
excerpt:
Max Verstappen will start the Las Vegas GP from pole position, despite qualifying behind Kimi Antonelli.

Max Verstappen has inherited pole position for the Las Vegas Grand Prix after qualifying in second, behind Kimi Antonelli, who has a grid drop.

Antonelli clinched pole after posting a 1m 33.893s on his final lap, some 0.258s clear of Verstappen. However, a power unit component change means the Italian starts sixth.

It promotes his team-mate George Russell onto the front row after the Briton qualified in third, ahead of Lando Norris and Isack Hadjar.

Ferrari suffered a complete disaster, with both Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton failing to make the final part of qualifying in Sin City.

Max Verstappen inherits Las Vegas pole as Ferrari suffer double elimination embarrassment

# Driver Team Time Tyre

Results are being loaded...

Q3 - Antonelli leaves it late

Following the opening hot laps in the final part of qualifying, it was Verstappen on provisional pole ahead of Norris.

Russell and Hadjar completed the top four, with the former requesting a tow from Antonelli, who has a five-place grid penalty.

Ahead of the final flying laps, several drivers jostled for position on the circuit to receive as strong a tow as possible, due to the significance of receiving one.

Both Red Bulls failed to improve, while Norris got within one-tenth of Verstappen, as did Russell. The final car across the line was Antonelli, who found a big improvement to claim pole by over two-tenths.

However, his grid penalty drops the world champion to sixth and promotes Verstappen to the front row.

© XPB Images

Q2 - Double Ferrari exit

It was a dramatic second part of qualifying which saw several big names need a late improvement to avoid being eliminated.

Verstappen was one of those, but comfortably improved to go quickest in Q2, remarkably ahead of Alpine's Pierre Gasly.

Unfortunately, both Ferraris failed to make the cut. Leclerc made a costly mistake on his final lap, while Hamilton struggled for grip.

It marked an embarrassing moment for the Scuderia, with Leclerc and Hamilton qualifying in 11th and 12th, Nico Hulkenberg 13th, Carlos Sainz 14th, Gabriel Bortoleto 15th and Alex Albon 16th.

© XPB Images

Q1 - Lewis Hamilton struggles

Qualifying got underway in dry conditions, with track evolution being significant at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit.

The cool conditions worked well for Mercedes in the first part of qualifying, as Russell topped Q1 from Antonelli.

It was the usual names towards the top, except Hamilton, who struggled to improve as the circuit became quicker, progressing to Q2 down in 13th.

As for the elimination places, no real shocks took place. Rafael Camara had to settle for 17th, ahead of Sergio Perez, Fernando Alonso, Lance Stroll, Valtteri Bottas and Oliver Bearman.
